title: Mercury
subtitle: Closest planet to the Sun
essay:
Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. Its orbit is the most eccentric of the eight planets, carrying it between 46 and 70 million km from the Sun. It rotates exactly three times for every two orbits, so one solar day, from sunrise to sunrise, lasts about 176 Earth days, twice as long as its year.

With almost no atmosphere to hold heat, Mercury has the widest temperature range of any planet: the sunlit side exceeds 400 °C while the night side falls to about −180 °C. The surface is heavily cratered, like the Moon's, but Mercury's high density of 5,429 kg/m³ shows that a large iron core makes up most of its interior. Mariner 10 flew past three times in 1974 and 1975, and MESSENGER orbited from 2011 to 2015, mapping the whole planet and finding water ice in permanently shadowed craters near the poles.

Because it never appears more than about 28° from the Sun, Mercury is seen only low in the twilight sky, after sunset or before sunrise, near its greatest elongations. It looks like a bright star, reaching magnitude −2.4, and a small telescope shows its changing phase.

title: Venus
subtitle: Second planet from the Sun
essay:
Venus is close to Earth in size, with 95 percent of its radius and 82 percent of its mass, but its surface conditions are very different. A carbon dioxide atmosphere with a surface pressure of 92 bar traps heat so effectively that the average surface temperature is 464 °C, hotter than the day side of Mercury. Clouds of sulfuric acid cover the planet completely, so its surface has been mapped by radar, most thoroughly by NASA's Magellan orbiter from 1990 to 1994. The Soviet Venera landers returned the only photographs taken on the surface.

Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets, once every 243 Earth days, which is longer than its 225-day year. Together these give a solar day of about 117 Earth days. Magellan's radar maps show volcanic plains, large shield volcanoes and relatively few impact craters, which points to a geologically young surface.

After the Sun and the Moon, Venus is the brightest natural object in the sky, reaching magnitude −4.8. It appears as the evening or morning star, never more than about 47° from the Sun. Binoculars or a small telescope show its phases, which change from a small, nearly full disk to a large, thin crescent as Venus comes closer to Earth.

image.caption: Global view of the surface of Venus centred at 180° east longitude, built from Magellan radar data.

title: Earth
subtitle: Third planet from the Sun
essay:
Earth is the largest of the four rocky planets and the only world known to have liquid water on its surface and life. Oceans cover about 71 percent of the surface. The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with a surface pressure of about 1 bar, and the average surface temperature is 15 °C.

Earth's mean density of 5,513 kg/m³ is the highest of any planet. It reflects an iron-nickel core, and motion in the liquid outer core generates a global magnetic field. The field and the atmosphere together shield the surface from much of the solar wind and cosmic radiation; where charged particles reach the upper atmosphere near the magnetic poles, they produce aurorae. The crust is divided into plates that move a few centimetres a year, building mountains and recycling old crust into the mantle.

The seasons come from the 23.44° tilt of Earth's axis, not from changes in its distance from the Sun; Earth is in fact closest to the Sun in early January. The planet turns once relative to the stars in 23 h 56 m, and the extra four minutes in a 24-hour solar day come from its movement along its orbit. Its one natural satellite, the Moon, is large compared with the planet it orbits.

image.caption: Earth photographed by the Apollo 17 crew on 7 December 1972, showing Africa, Arabia and the Antarctic ice cap.

title: Mars
subtitle: Fourth planet from the Sun

facts.label: Surface pressure
facts.value: 6.36 mb at mean radius (4.0–8.7 mb by season)

essay:
Mars is about half Earth's diameter and has a tenth of its mass. Its thin carbon dioxide atmosphere has a mean surface pressure of about 6 millibar, under 1 percent of Earth's. Iron oxide in the dust gives the surface its red colour. Water ice is found in the polar caps and below the surface, and dry river valleys, deltas and lakebeds show that liquid water flowed there billions of years ago.

Mars has the largest volcano known in the solar system, Olympus Mons, and a canyon system, Valles Marineris, about 4,000 km long. Its day lasts 24 h 40 m and its axis is tilted 25°, close to Earth's, so it has seasons, each lasting about twice as long as Earth's because the Martian year is 1.88 Earth years. NASA's Perseverance rover is exploring Jezero Crater, an ancient lake basin, and collecting rock samples.

Mars reaches opposition about every 26 months, when it lies opposite the Sun and is visible all night. Near opposition it is a bright orange-red point, as bright as magnitude −2.9 at its best, and a small telescope can show a polar cap and dark surface markings. Its two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, are thought to be captured asteroids or debris from the early solar system.

image.caption: Mosaic of Viking Orbiter images showing Mars with the Valles Marineris canyon system across the centre.

title: Jupiter
subtitle: Fifth planet from the Sun
essay:
Jupiter is the largest planet, with 318 times the mass of Earth, more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined. It is a gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium and has no solid surface. Deep inside, the hydrogen is compressed into a liquid that conducts electricity, and this generates a magnetic field much stronger than Earth's. Jupiter rotates in under 10 hours, the shortest day of any planet, and the fast spin flattens it at the poles and draws its clouds into parallel belts and zones.

The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has been observed for more than 150 years and has been shrinking. Jupiter also has faint rings, found by Voyager 1 in 1979. Galileo discovered the four largest moons in 1610: Io, the most volcanically active body in the solar system; Europa, which probably has a liquid water ocean under its ice; Ganymede, which is larger than Mercury; and Callisto. NASA's Juno spacecraft went into orbit around Jupiter in 2016, and Europa Clipper launched in 2024.

Jupiter is usually the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon and Venus, reaching magnitude −2.9. Binoculars held steady show the Galilean moons as points of light in a line beside the planet, and a small telescope shows the cloud belts.

image.caption: True-colour mosaic of Jupiter from Cassini's narrow-angle camera, taken during its December 2000 flyby.

title: Saturn
subtitle: Sixth planet from the Sun
essay:
Saturn is the second-largest planet. Its mean density, 687 kg/m³, is the lowest of any planet and less than that of water. Like Jupiter it is made mostly of hydrogen and helium, and it rotates quickly, in about 10.7 hours. The spin makes Saturn the most flattened planet: its equatorial radius is about 10 percent larger than its polar radius.

The main rings span hundreds of thousands of kilometres but are mostly only about 10 metres thick. They are made of countless pieces of water ice, from grains to boulders, with a little rock and dust. Saturn has 293 confirmed moons, more than any other planet. Titan, the largest, has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane, and Enceladus vents water from an ocean beneath its south polar ice. The Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, and its Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005.

Saturn is easy to see with the unaided eye as a steady, yellowish point, usually between magnitude 0 and 1. A small telescope at 25× or more shows the rings. Because the planet's axis is tilted 26.7°, the angle at which we see the rings changes over its 29.5-year orbit; they were edge-on in 2025 and are now opening again.

image.caption: Saturn and its rings in natural colour, a Cassini mosaic released in 2008.

title: Uranus
subtitle: Seventh planet from the Sun
essay:
Uranus was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781. It is an ice giant: under an atmosphere of hydrogen, helium and methane lies a dense fluid of water, methane and ammonia surrounding a small rocky core. Methane in the upper atmosphere absorbs red light, which gives the planet its blue-green colour.

The rotation axis is tilted 97.77°, so Uranus effectively rolls along its orbit on its side. Over its 84-year orbit, each pole has about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness. A giant collision early in the planet's history is the usual explanation for the tilt. Uranus rotates in 17 h 14 m, in the retrograde direction. It has 13 known rings, mostly narrow and dark, and 29 recognised moons named after characters in the works of Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited, flying past in 1986.

Near opposition Uranus reaches magnitude 5.4 to 5.6, at the limit of naked-eye visibility under a dark sky, and it is easy to locate in binoculars with a finder chart. A telescope shows a small, featureless greenish disk about 3.8 arcseconds across.

title: Neptune
subtitle: Eighth planet from the Sun
essay:
Neptune was the first planet found by prediction rather than by searching. Urbain Le Verrier calculated its position from small irregularities in the motion of Uranus, and Johann Galle found it in 1846 within about a degree of the predicted place. It is an ice giant, slightly smaller than Uranus but more massive and denser. It takes 164.8 years to orbit the Sun and completed its first orbit since discovery in 2011.

Neptune has the fastest winds measured on any planet, over 2,000 km/h. Voyager 2, the only spacecraft to visit, flew past in 1989 and photographed the Great Dark Spot, a storm about the size of Earth that had disappeared by the time the Hubble Space Telescope looked in 1994. The planet has five main rings, which are faint and clumpy, and 16 recognised moons. The largest, Triton, orbits in the direction opposite to Neptune's rotation, which suggests it was captured from the Kuiper Belt, and Voyager saw geyser-like plumes on its frozen nitrogen surface.

At magnitude 7.7, Neptune is too faint for the unaided eye but visible in binoculars with a finder chart. A small telescope at high magnification shows a tiny bluish disk about 2.3 arcseconds across.

image.caption: Neptune from Voyager 2 in August 1989, showing the Great Dark Spot and its bright companion cloud.
